endings.text: End of the walk. W. W. Kimball died on 16 December 1904, and John Glessner crossed Eighteenth Street to stand among his honorary pallbearers. The Reading Class went on. It met every Monday from October to May, "until 1930". When Frances Glessner died, her husband tried to say who she had been. "She had a clean and wholesome and orderly mind, a heart overflowing with love for family and friends and for all in any need." That is the house in one sentence: clean, wholesome, orderly, and full of people you never see.

evidence.text: Passers-by remarked on the narrow windows in the north side along 18th Street, just enough to light the narrow corridors, not realizing that on the courtyard side Richardson had put generous windows.

evidence.locator: HABS data pages pp. 1-2; the museum's Richardson page.
evidence.text: HABS dates the building from June 1, 1886 to December 1, 1887; the house museum gives Richardson's death as April 26, 1886.
George Pullman, across the street, complained of the Glessner house: 'I do not know what I have ever done to have that thing staring me in the face every time I go out of my door'.
Glessner built at the corner of Eighteenth Street and Prairie Avenue, diagonally opposite Pullman's mansion.

Monday at the Fortress: the day, Monday 21 November 1904, the hour and the order of the walk are this jaunt's framing, chosen because the stories meet on it (three days after Arthur Caton's death, a Monday of the Reading Class, before Kimball's death in December). No visit on that day is asserted.

Monday at the Fortress: who is seen at each stop, where they stand, what they do and when are reconstructed. People with cards in the town play themselves; people the town has no card for (and the unnamed servants, callers and passers-by) are unnamed figures in period dress, and no likeness is claimed. No word anyone says is asserted.

evidence.locator: The biography of Frances Macbeth Glessner.
evidence.text: In 1893 William Rainey Harper, president of the University of Chicago, asked Frances Glessner for advice on how to introduce faculty wives to women of the city. The result was her Monday Morning Reading Class, which met for two hours in the library of the house every Monday from October to May. During the first hour the women sewed and listened to a professional reader; during the second there was lighter reading or a lecture. Membership was by invitation only, and the class continued until 1930.

Frances Glessner founded the Monday Morning Reading Class in the house; its weekly meetings ran through the winters and springs, in the library, and while the reading went on the ladies' fingers were busy with sewing.
Yellow glass under chipped white glass in the door leading to the courtyard gives the hall a feeling of sunlight even in cloudy weather.
There are two or more entrances or exits to every principal room, and passages are so planned that servants rarely are in evidence.
The Virginia creeper on the courtyard walls was carried from the old house; one vine fifty-five feet long was replanted and trained its full length, and it flourished.

evidence.locator: The biography of Frances Macbeth Glessner.
evidence.text: In 1904 Frances Glessner set up a workbench in the basement of Glessner House and began producing simple and elegant objects; her pieces bear her hallmark, 'a G encircling a honeybee', for her bee keeping. She studied with Annibale Fogliata, a master jewelry craftsman of Hull House, and Madeline Yale Wynne, a noted Chicago silversmith.

opening.text:
JAUNT: MONDAY AT THE FORTRESS. Monday morning, 21 November 1904, at the corner of Eighteenth Street and Prairie Avenue.

Five stops in and around the Glessner House. Today is a Monday, which means the Reading Class: the wives of University of Chicago professors and the ladies of the South Side, gathering in the library at the invitation of Frances Glessner. Inside these walls everything runs like a clock, and servants are rarely seen. Across Eighteenth Street, in the house of the piano king, the clock is running down.

Start at the corner, where the neighbours first saw what Richardson had built.

armour_corwith_house_1945_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists Mrs. Henry Corwith here. Before them, the Armour household lived here (1890-1891).

armour_house_2115_prairie.text: A stone house with a steep mansard roof, built for the lumberman David Kelley. The family of the meatpacker Philip D. Armour lived here for nearly 50 years. Armour's widow was one of the last people living on the street.

buckingham_house_2036_prairie.text: Clarence Buckingham's house in the 1904 Blue Book. In 1927 his sister Kate will give Chicago the Buckingham Fountain in his memory, its centre jet throwing water 150 feet up.

coleman_ames_house_1811_prairie.text: A Romanesque house of rough brown sandstone, built in 1886 for Joseph G. Coleman. Cobb and Frost were the architects. It still stands.

dent_house_1823_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists Thomas Dent here, a lawyer by the 1900 census.

dexter_house_1721_prairie.text: Wirt Dexter's house of 1863, given a new front by Arthur Little in 1889. By 1904 the Blue Book lists Henry H. Walker here.

dexter_house_1721_prairie_frame_house.text: Wirt Dexter's frame house of 1863, the first house on this lot. Arthur Little's brick front on Prairie Avenue was built onto its street end; the old house's own front, porch and bay windows, faces the side yard.

edson_keith_house_1906_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists Mrs. Edson Keith here.

elbridge_keith_house_1900_prairie.text: A limestone house with a steep slate roof, built for Elbridge Keith, a hat merchant who became a banker. The top floor inside that roof was added in the 1880s. It is the last Second Empire house left on Prairie Avenue.

fort_dearborn_massacre_monument_1893.text: A bronze group by Carl Rohl-Smith, paid for by George M. Pullman and set up beside his house in 1893. It shows the Potawatomi leader Black Partridge saving Margaret Helm during the battle of August 1812.

george_glessner_house_1706_prairie.text: Home of George M. Glessner, son of the granite house at 1800; the Glessners built it beside his sister's house at 1700.

glessner_house.text: A granite fortress on the street, with a sunny courtyard inside. People passing by remarked on its narrow windows along 18th Street, not knowing the big ones face the courtyard. By 1904 John and Frances Glessner had lived here since 1887.

glessner_lee_house_1700_prairie.text: Built by the Glessners for their daughter Frances, who married Blewett Lee in 1898. Decades on she will build the Nutshell Studies of Unexplained Death, tiny crime scenes still used to train investigators.

goodman_house_1612_prairie.text: Joseph Goodman's stone Italianate of 1869, two years before the Great Fire: round-headed windows under long keystones, and an arched portico at the top of a high stoop.

henderson_house_1816_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists Mrs. Charles M. Henderson here. Before them, W. H. Merrill jr. lived here (1899-1903).

hibbard_house_1701_prairie.text: William G. Hibbard's house of 1869, by William Le Baron Jenney, who fifteen years later built the Home Insurance Building, called the first skyscraper.

premise: Every Monday from October to May the ladies of Chicago come to the stone fortress at Eighteenth and Prairie to sew and listen. This Monday the house across the street is waiting for a death.

stage.caption: Ladies come down Prairie Avenue in twos for the Monday class.

cast.name: A member of the Reading Class (unnamed)
A second member of the class (unnamed)
A professor's wife, new to the class (unnamed)

stops.text: The corner of Eighteenth and Prairie. The house is granite, low and hard, with windows on the street side barely wide enough to light a corridor. Its architect, H. H. Richardson, died in 1886 before it was finished; it went up between June 1886 and December 1887. Not everyone liked it. George Pullman, just across the way, complained: "I do not know what I have ever done to have that thing staring me in the face every time I go out of my door". Pullman is seven years dead now, and the house is still staring. What the passers-by never see is the other side: generous windows onto a sunny courtyard, and a household that runs like a machine. The ladies are arriving on foot.

stage.caption: Frances Glessner greets her guests at the door while Christine Nelson stands behind her.

cast.name: A member of the Reading Class (unnamed)
A second member of the class (unnamed)

stops.text: The front door. In 1893 William Rainey Harper, the president of the new University of Chicago, asked Frances Glessner how the professors' wives might meet the women of the city. Her answer was this: the Monday Morning Reading Class. It meets in the library for two hours every Monday from October to May. For the first hour the ladies sew while a professional reader reads aloud; the second hour is lighter, a reading or a lecture. Nobody joins by asking. "Membership was by invitation only", and for a professor's wife new to Chicago an invitation is the way in. Mrs. Glessner greets her guests herself. Christine Nelson, the parlor maid, stands ready for their wraps. Then the door shuts, and the house does what it was built to do.

stage.caption: Below the hall bay, the household works out of sight: a maid crosses the court with a tray, and the cook waits at the service door.

stops.text: Inside, the house turns its back on the street and opens to the courtyard. The door to the court has yellow glass under chipped white glass, which gives the hall "a feeling of sunlight even in cloudy weather", and today is cloudy. The plan is a puzzle box: every principal room has two or more ways in and out, and the passages are "so planned that servants rarely are in evidence". So while the needles go in and out in the library, a whole second household is moving round them unseen: the cook, the maids, the man who keeps the fires. Frances Glessner wanted a house where the work never showed. She got one. The ladies sew. The reader reads. And the help keeps out of sight in the court, where only you can see them.

stage.caption: August Billings brings the coal up from the cellar and stops at the stair to look toward the street.

stops.text: The service stair, down to the basement. Down there is the newest room in the house: the workbench Frances Glessner set up this year, where she makes silver with a hammer and a torch and stamps each piece with "a G encircling a honeybee". Upstairs she is the most correct hostess in Chicago. Downstairs she is a craftsman taking lessons from a Hull House jeweller. Both are true, and she has been running this house, and that class, by the clock for eleven years. But across Eighteenth Street a neighbour has been ill for a long time, and this morning the doctor is calling again. Look out through the gates toward the corner house: the house of William W. Kimball, the piano maker.

stage.caption: A doctor climbs the Kimball steps; Ernest Sibbald, the steward, opens the door, and Mrs. Kimball waits in the hall.

stops.text: 1801 Prairie, across Eighteenth Street: the Kimball house. William Wallace Kimball came to Chicago in 1857 and traded his Iowa land for four pianos, which he sold from a second-floor office. Now his factory turns out about a hundred pianos and organs a week, and his name is on pianos all over America. He and his wife Evaline have no children. And he is dying. He will die "at home after a lingering illness" on 16 December, and his funeral will be held in this house. Watch the doctor going up the steps, and the steward who lets him in. Among his honorary pallbearers will be "Marshall Field, Robert T. Lincoln" and, from the house of the Reading Class, "J. J. Glessner".
